summary: This document explains how to interconnect a pair of TRILL switch ports using pseudowires, under existing TRILL and PWE3 standards.

plainLanguage.summary: Two special switches far apart need to behave as if joined by a cable. This explains how to use a virtual cable run through another network.

questions: how to carry trill over mpls
what ppp code points does trill use
why use a ppp pseudowire for trill
subtitle: How to make two TRILL switch ports behave as if a single cable joined them, by running a PPP pseudowire across an MPLS or IP network.

tldr.problem: Two TRILL switches may sit far apart, with a packet-switched network between them, yet TRILL wants them to look like neighbors on one link.
tldr.mechanism: A PPP pseudowire (type 0x0007) joins the two switch ports, so TRILL Data and TRILL IS-IS packets travel as TRILL over PPP over the pseudowire, with the existing PPP code points 0x005d and 0x405d.
tldr.outcome: No new pseudowire standard is needed. The RFC also sets priority rules for control traffic, notes the MTU effect, and recommends link security below TRILL rather than PPP security.

today: RFC 7173 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links, RFC 6325) routes data frames optimally between pairs of devices in networks of any shape, without configuration. Devices that speak TRILL are called TRILL switches or Routing Bridges (RBridges).

Links between TRILL switches can use many link protocols, such as Ethernet or PPP. RFC 7173 specifies how to interconnect a pair of TRILL switch ports with a pseudowire, using only existing TRILL and PWE3 (Pseudowire Emulation End-to-End) standards.
sections.plainLanguage: TRILL switches need a link between them. This RFC says how to make that link out of a pretend wire that crosses another network.

sections.title: Joining Two TRILL Ports with a Pseudowire
sections.content:
The pseudowire used is a PPP pseudowire, described in RFC 4618. It can be signaled (RFC 4447) or manually configured. The TRILL switch ports at the two ends act as native service processing elements and, when the pseudowire runs over MPLS or IP, as label switched or IP routers.

Pseudowires give transparent transport, so the two ports look directly interconnected by a transparent link. TRILL adjacency is then discovered and established automatically through TRILL IS-IS control messages. The pseudowire rides in a packet switched network tunnel, for example an MPLS or MPLS-TP label switched path, and this application needs no additions to existing pseudowire standards.

For the PPP pseudowire type, the PW type is 0x0007. Once the pseudowire is up and TRILL use is negotiated within PPP, the two ports appear connected by a PPP link. If the connection is signaled, the initiating port MUST attempt setup with pseudowire type PPP (0x0007). Behavior otherwise follows TRILL over PPP in RFC 6361.
sections.plainLanguage: The two switches talk through a pretend wire. Once it is set up, they think they are plugged straight into each other and say hello the usual way.

sections.title: Priority and Packet Size
sections.content:
The sending port SHOULD map the inner priority of TRILL Data packets to the Traffic Class field of the pseudowire label (RFC 5462), so that high priority data is less likely to be discarded when lots of low priority data arrives.

Control traffic gets better treatment. TRILL IS-IS Hello and MTU PDUs, which are critical to establishing and maintaining adjacency, SHOULD be sent with the MPLS Traffic Class that calls for maximum priority. Other TRILL IS-IS PDUs SHOULD use the highest priority below the maximum. TRILL Data packets SHOULD use Traffic Classes below those used for TRILL IS-IS PDUs. This lowers the chance that other traffic causes a false loss of adjacency.

On size: if a pseudowire supports fragmentation and reassembly, which the RFC says has received little or no deployment, there is no reason to do TRILL MTU testing and the pseudowire does not constrain the campus-wide MTU size. If it does not support fragmentation, the more common case, the available TRILL IS-IS packet payload size over the pseudowire (counting MPLS encapsulation with a control word), or some lower value, MUST be used when determining the MTU size.

MPLS label switched routers between the two ports have no awareness of TRILL and will not change the TRILL Header hop count.
sections.plainLanguage: Hello messages that keep the link alive go in the express lane so heavy traffic cannot make the switches think the link broke. Packets also have to fit through the pretend wire.

sections.title: Packets on the Pseudowire
sections.content:
In the MPLS case, with no TRILL Header extensions, a TRILL Data packet carries server MPLS tunnel labels (4 octets per label), a 4-octet PW label, a 4-octet control word, a 2-octet PPP header of 0x005d, the 6-octet TRILL Header, the destination and source MAC addresses (6 octets each), a data label of 4 or 8 octets, and the payload body. The data label is the VLAN Label or Fine-Grained Label (RFC 7172) of the payload.

A TRILL IS-IS packet has the same outer labels, PW label and control word, then a PPP header of 0x405d, an 8-octet Common IS-IS Header, the PDU type specific header and the IS-IS TLVs. The PPP header values for the two packet kinds are specified in RFC 6361.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet is like a letter in several envelopes. A small tag on the inside says whether it is real data or a control message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TRILL-level security, such as authentication of TRILL IS-IS PDUs, is not affected by the link technology. Link security below the TRILL level could come from PPP security, pseudowire security, MPLS or IP security, or the security of the underlying link technology.

The PPP layer here is described as somewhat vestigial: it exists mainly as a convenient way to reuse existing PPP code points to identify TRILL Data and TRILL IS-IS packets, and existing PPP security standards are arguably questionable by current criteria. So it is NOT RECOMMENDED to use PPP security, and it is RECOMMENDED that link security be provided at the MPLS or IP layer or the link layer below. For sensitive data, end-to-end security between end stations should also be considered. Risks of carrying point-to-point protocols over a packet switched network are discussed in RFC 3985.
sections.plainLanguage: The padlock should go on the outer tunnel, not on the thin inner PPP wrapper. For secrets, lock the message itself too.

sections.title: Why PPP and Not Another Pseudowire Type
sections.content:
An informative appendix says Ethernet pseudowires (RFC 4448) could carry TRILL without change, but this would add 12 or 16 bytes per packet within the payload, because the TRILL hop MAC addresses, optional tags and the Ethertype (0x22f3 for TRILL Data, 0x22f4 for Layer 2 IS-IS) are needed.

A new pseudowire type for TRILL could also be defined, but the authors judged that any efficiency gain over PPP pseudowires would be too small to justify the complexity. Using PPP also means any traffic dissector that understands TRILL PPP encoding and PPP pseudowires can decode TRILL carried this way.
sections.plainLanguage: They could have invented a new kind of wire, but reusing an existing one was simpler and almost as good.
